description: The raccoon, referred to as <DW53>, is described as genteel and mindful of good manners, admitting he did not mean anything unkind and apologizing to Cracker. He claims he put a leftover piece of squash pie in the cupboard for lunch, which he describes as lovely, after consuming a large amount of bread, honey, and milk. <DW53> feels unhappy because he did not save the pie for dinner and claims he was working all morning due to hunger, correcting that he worked like a raccoon. The bear notes that <DW53> is restless when tired, in dull weather, or when <DW53> is trying, and believes he would not like the Madam to be disturbed. The two little brown mice discover a crack in the cupboard, enlarge it with their teeth, and find a large piece of squash pie, which they immediately eat. The grandmother affirms <DW53> did not mean anything and believes he has a good heart.

Eily goes to the forest to gather shticks and encounters a Grane Man resembling hoppergrass caught in a spider's wib; he grants her a wish to have anything in the world, and as she speaks, pearls and diamonds fall from her mouth and hop across the cabin floor. Her mother, Honor Macarthy, believes Eily is bewitched and claims she speaks buttons, pressing her hand over Eily’s mouth to stop her. Phelim finds the shining objects, calls her father Dennis Macarthy, who examines them and identifies them as jewels, not buttons. Dennis, skeptical of the bewitchment, sends Eily to Doctor O'Shaughnessy, who confirms the objects are jewels and dismisses the supernatural claims. Eily, who had heard fairy stories from her mother, is excited by the encounter and considers wishes like a magic carpet or golden goose. The family is unsettled, with Honor accusing Eily of stealing the Countess’s beads, but the doctor ultimately accepts the situation and takes Eily away.

The boy carries the Golden Dragon to the temple, covers it with a crimson silk sash, and exits quietly, noting the priests are snoring calmly, indicating the wine worked. He later fights the old cat, using teeth, nails, and fists, with the cat attacking with spread claws and a tail as large as the boy’s arm; the fight ends when the boy grabs the cat by the throat, and their teeth meet in the boy’s arm. Uncle Munkle expresses concern about Cracker’s association with Mrs. Cow, a domestic animal, and questions Cracker’s diet and teeth, suspecting poor nutrition, though he later shows interest after learning about almonds. The raccoon and Bruin observe a fight between the boy and the old cat, with the raccoon praising it and criticizing Bruin for stopping it. The parrot attacks a man, who is attacked by a heavy body with teeth and claws. Toto bought almonds from a pedler and would give them to Uncle Munkle if asked.

The bear, Mr. Bruin, accompanies Toto on a long walk carrying a large basket of food for their own lunch, while Toto carries medicines. Bruin expresses discomfort with his appearance, believing he is frightfully ugly, though Toto insists he is a perfect beauty. The old man, Mr. Hermit, initially misidentifies a black, large figure as a boy or a "Caesar or Pompey," but Toto corrects him, stating the person is Mr. Bruin. A crow reveals Mr. Hermit is ill, broken-leg, refusing food, and fearing death. The wood-pigeon, moved by the sorrow, brings leaves that revive Mr. Hermit, who then calls for "food," which Bruin and Toto provide. The wood-pigeon later comforts the group, and after a moment of despair, Mr. Hermit welcomes them, saying he was glad to meet them. The bear, initially shy, is deeply affected by the situation and later withdraws in sorrow. The wood-pigeon and parrot remain content in their perches.

Eileen Macarthy, a child in Ireland, receives a fairy charm from a Green Man who appears on a yellow toadstool at the foot of an oak tree. The charm, activated by the phrase "Slanegher Banegher, Skeen na Lane," grants her wishes but brings her misery as she is forced to speak endlessly and drop jewels. She initially mistakes a tiny green man in a scarlet cap, caught in a spider’s web, for a grasshopper, but saves him, realizing he is a living being. The Green Man, who is not a priest, acknowledges the charm’s power and teaches her that kindness and gentle words are valuable. He warns that the gift will only end when she returns to the same spot with holly and the same phrase. He tells her to hold onto the jewels as they are her last, and that fairy gifts are now rare, as few believe in the Green Men. After a day of hardship, Eileen escapes her prison, filled with wonder, and returns home, having learned that every kind deed is a diamond.

The kitchen is a warm, lively space with clean white walls decorated with wreaths, garlands, and fir-boughs emitting a warm, spicy fragrance. All metal items, including the kettle, are polished to shine, reflecting the fire’s glow. The tea-kettle, made of copper and brightly burnished, sings merrily, puffs steam, and expresses pride in its position, stating that usefulness is sufficient and not everyone can be beautiful. It feels transformed into golden metal and remarks on its rare appearance, though it is seen by the raccoon as a black and cracked pot. The raccoon, who initially claims the kettle is not alive, later believes it is alive due to a critical incident where it poured boiling water over a robber’s legs. The raccoon fears the kettle, having once believed it removed its paw skin, and is unsettled by its movements. The fire reflects the kettle’s glow and admires it, and the room is warm, with a smooth floor and a scent suggesting food. Bruin maintains order by raking the fire, filling the kettle, and securing doors and windows before sleeping. The kitchen is a central, active space where daily tasks, conversations, and interactions occur.

Toto and the bear visit a cave where a crow lives, having heard of the old hermit’s accident; the hermit is found lying in a dimly lit cavern, barely alive, and is given water by a bear named Bruin. The cave is illuminated by torches and glow-worms, with a festive atmosphere, and guests including a squirrel, raccoon, and others gather to enjoy stories. Toto requests Mr. Baldhead to tell a fairy story, which the hermit agrees to after noting the boy’s fondness for tales. The squirrel claims the well-known rhyme "Hey diddle diddle" is a lie, offering a different version. The woodmouse reveals his son Prick-ear is to be married the next evening, which the raccoon learns only after being asked; the raccoon criticizes the timing and offers to attend with music. The woodmouse expresses delight and asks Toto and the raccoon to bring Cracker and others, noting they have engaged the cave for the wedding due to their large family. The old hermit is confined to the cave after breaking his leg, and the group shares a joyful, though somewhat chaotic, gathering.

The Emperor, Wah-Song, is haunted by the Golden Dragon, which calls him by name and commands him with terrifying authority, causing him to panic and lose control. The Dragon, with ruby eyes, a crowned head, and long talons, accuses Wah-Song of neglecting his duties, particularly for sending half-rotten pineapples instead of fresh melons, which were brought by Ly-Chee every Tuesday for thirty years. The Emperor condemns Ly-Chee to death unless the Dragon descends and begs for his life, but the Dragon declares it comes not to beg but to command. As a result, Wah-Song agrees to send Ly-Chee a free pardon before daybreak, twenty bags of ducats—one per hour in prison—and appoints him Chief Sweeper for life with gilded brooms and ivory handles, plus his son Chop-Chin as Second Sweeper. This leads to a joyful procession where Ly-Chee and his family celebrate. Later, when the Emperor is unannounced, Ly-Chee drenches the Emperor’s clothing with ice-cold water, leading to a public humiliation and the Emperor’s complaint about wet shoes and a saturated petticoat.

Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy, a physician and captor of the child Eileen Macarthy, claims to have a supernatural power and declares he will become King of Ireland before the month ends. He imprisons Eileen in a large bare room, forces her to speak continuously, and asserts that she has met a "Grane Man" who granted her a wish, which he now possesses. He threatens her with physical punishment if she speaks "Bliss ye!" and promises her a sweet-cake upon return. His wife, Mrs. O'Shaughnessy, is bewildered by his claims and the jewels he claims are from Eileen’s mouth, which he says are bits of glass that hop and leap. The woman believes him delusional, and he reacts with rage when she challenges his assertions. Eileen, terrified, believes he is mad, and after a period of silence, is forced to speak again. Dr. O'Shaughnessy leaves after making his wife promise to keep Eileen in constant conversation. The story ends with the sound of a gig and the doctor’s arrival at his home, suggesting the events are part of a larger, fantastical narrative involving Ireland, magic, and delusion.

The parrot, Miss Mary, is a dignified and observant bird who resents being overlooked, particularly by Master Cracker, whom she mocks for his flirtatious behavior. She claims her father, Polacko, was a noble bird captured in China, where he lived for twenty years with a mandarin, enjoying freedom and chow-chow, before leaving to return to Africa due to outrage over being forced to eat with chopsticks. Miss Mary recalls losing two feathers from her tail, which were bitten off while asleep, and expresses sorrow over Polacko’s departure. She is often seen watching the window, missing the wood-pigeon, and is known for her sharp wit, such as questioning cows’ intelligence and commenting on the bear’s ears. The man, a thief who enters the cottage, is caught by Miss Mary when he steals silver teaspoons, prompting her to shout "Stop thief!" and later falsely claims the "robber" is Mrs. <DW53> with an acquaintance. The squirrel, Toto, and the bear interact in playful chaos, including a fall that ruins a custard pie, and the bear later claims Master Cracker is tickling his ear. Miss Mary remains calm and composed, offering stories and maintaining a quiet authority among the group.

The High Cellarer, a royal officer, is arrested by the King for having black soot-stained hands and possessing sapphires and the key to the treasure-chamber, which proves his guilt. The King, known for his riches and kindness, places a coal in his pocket, which later speaks and warns him of danger. The coal, when placed beside the bed, burns fiercely and warns the High Cellarer, who flees and spends the night shivering. The King later places the coal on the table beside his bed, where it speaks three times, saving the treasure and revealing the thief’s identity. The princess, when presented with rubies and sapphires, impresses the King with her beauty and eyes, causing him to fall in love. The King, after being startled by the princess’s question about butter, is humbled. The coal, after being placed in the king’s waistcoat, becomes black and dead within ten minutes, and is later rubbed over the treasure-chamber door. The High Cellarer attempts to steal the key but is burned by the coal, causing him to fall on the hearth. The King rewards the High Cellarer with a ruby ring.

Pigeon Pretty, a wood-pigeon, is pursued by a large hawk and falls fainting at Bruin's feet; the hawk is then pounced on by something or someone, enveloped in a thick white covering that entangles his claws, binds his wings, and nearly stifles him, before being seized and lifted into the air by Bruin, who confronts him with a stern voice. The hawk, face to face with Bruin, replies sullenly, "No! wring away." Later, the hawk is seen sitting on the hermit's knee, sipping broth and gracefully submitting to having his plumage stroked, while Pigeon Pretty sits on the hermit's other knee, fully recovered and beaming. The stranger, formerly sullen and fierce-eyed, transforms into a noble figure with bright, strangely bright eyes, smooth glossy plumage, and a proud head after being treated kindly by the hermit, who agrees with Pigeon Pretty that the hawk should be fed and released. Bruin, initially upset, laughs with the group after the incident, and the group departs, with Toto looking back with wide eyes, feeling the marbles in his pockets as soothing. The hermit is seen in a strange state, later revived by Pigeon Pretty's arrival.

Short-Tailed Comet No. 73, a young comet with a short bobbing tail, is given orders by the Comet Master to travel for thirteen weeks and three days, avoiding the Sun, Earth, and Planet Bungo, turning left when meeting other comets, and not speaking to meteors. He is excited by the freedom of space but becomes frustrated by the lack of purpose in his journey. He questions the reason for travel, learning from Long-Tail No. 45 that the Comet Master sent him but does not explain the purpose. After disobeying orders by speaking to a meteor, he is consumed by the Sun, which increases its fire and swallows him. The meteor witnesses the event, expresses shock and regret, and later forgets it. The Comet Master erases No. 73 from the list of short-tailed comets and assigns another comet, No. 1 Express, to travel and arrest a runaway meteor with red face and blue hair, to be sent to Planet Bungo for reform. The Sun, the Comet Master, and the court-yard are central to the comets' lives, with the Master maintaining order through a long stick and the Sun consuming comets. The old comet warns that only the Master and Sun know the true reason for travel, which remains unexplained.

Eileen, a young woman, is carried into a tall, dark, gloomy house resembling the green-spectacled doctor after a drive of some miles. Mrs. O'Shaughnessy, the house's wife, emerges from the kitchen, wipes her hands on her apron, and recognizes Eileen as "Honor Macarthy's Eily," exclaiming in astonishment. Eileen recounts a story involving an old woman, Moira Magoyle, and her animals, then reveals her fairy gift: diamonds and pearls fall from her lips in showers, which she catches in her apron, ending up with more than a quart of large, pea-sized gems. The gems fall fast and faster, filling her lap and the room, which becomes ankle-deep, and Mrs. O'Shaughnessy, frightened and cross, piles them up, muttering "Michael knows best" and feeling a strange sense of blissing. Eileen claims she will miss the doctor, whom she describes as "agrayable," and Mrs. O'Shaughnessy agrees, noting he is so only when he wants to be. Eileen returns home with her apron full of pearls and diamonds, which she later shares with her husband, the Count of Kilmoggan, becoming a rich woman.

The grandmother tells a story passed down from her grandmother, "The Story of Chop-Chin and the Golden Dragon," which is considered always true due to being told by two grandmothers in succession. She begins knitting after telling the story and settles into her chair, where the little squirrel attends her, picking up yarn and bringing her food. The squirrel finds comfort in the warm interior of the forest, especially during snowing weather. Toto explains that heavenly bodies have tails, move rapidly despite appearing stationary, and get milk from the Milky Way; he is mocked by the raccoon for lacking details but agrees to provide more. Toto recounts a storm in the forest where he was safe in a hollow, threatened by a cat named Klawtobitz who demanded he leave her tree, citing her seven-year occupancy. Toto defends himself by claiming he is dry while she is wet. Toto and Bruin enter the house with milk-pails, sit by the fire, and are greeted by the raccoon, who mocks Toto and claims to be sweeping the hearth. The raccoon expresses hope that Madam will visit the forest, bringing knitting and gingerbread, and learn to love it as Toto does. The bear had dancing-school the previous night and still feels its effects, recommending a story instead. The raccoon says the brown mice are a great annoyance to Madam and all, and that Madam opposes killing creatures. The grandmother announces bedtime when the clock strikes nine.

At a lively forest assembly, hundreds of small guests, including a raccoon and a boy, cause initial confusion and terror, prompting the bride—dressed in a brown fur travelling-dress and carried by her father—to nearly faint. The bridegroom, a small red mouse, reacts with fierce protectiveness. Mr. Woodmouse Senior remains calm, greeting the guests warmly as Mr. <DW53>, Mr. Toto, and Cracker. Toto whistles while circling, his scarlet neck-tie waving like a banner, while a mole expresses interest in food, noting dancing does not satisfy hunger. Supper is served in the side-cave and includes various nuts, acorns, berries, and golden corn from the field-cousins. A man accidentally buries a mole in a pyramid of hazel-nuts, leading to its rescue. The meal is described as exceptional and highly appetizing, with the star-nosed mole delivering a discourse before the ceremony. After the event, the family gathers, and the bride and groom leave for their home under an elder-bush. The raccoon is praised for his grace in greeting, and the mole, though initially excluded from the dance, is later seen enjoying the food. A prior incident involving Mr. <DW53> chasing Prick-ear is recalled, though it is later softened by the belief that Mr. <DW53> now has kind feelings for the family.

The woodchuck, known as Chucky, is a central figure in the winter gathering, found sleeping in a ball of brown fur enclosed in a knitted covering within a small cupboard near the fireplace, which also contains three blue ginger-jars filled with scarlet alder-berries and a great pewter tankard. He had difficulty accepting the new winter arrangement and was initially entangled in worsted covering, causing a commotion when the cupboard was opened. A long-drawn sound resembling a snort, squeal, and snore, originating from the cupboard, startled the group, leading to the bear’s laughter and the hermit drawing out the woodchuck. Chucky is described as warm and comfortable but deeply asleep, with no awareness of his surroundings. The bear’s shaggy coat was brushed during a vigorous scrubbing-dance that cleaned the floor and made it shine, while a red rose from the sunniest window was stuck in Bruin’s ear. Chucky’s aunt is also asleep and unreachable. The gathering includes Toto, Bruin, the squirrel, raccoon, crow, and hermit, who share stories and games after tea.

Toto, a pleasant-appearing boy, cries out "EGGS! eggs!" and jumps into the barn, waving a basket, asking Mrs. Speckle, Mrs. Spanish, and Dame Clucket for fresh eggs. Despite Dame Clucket’s explanation that she doesn’t have eggs that day because she wants to set them, Toto insists he hasn’t had eggs for two or three days and pleads for some, with both Mrs. Speckle and Dame Clucket agreeing he cannot be refused due to his kind demeanor. Toto later finds the shed piled high with kindling-wood, exclaims it would last ten years, and urges the bear to leave, claiming Granny wants him. The bear responds with comments about the new calf increasing butter production and the pig growing too large, asserting only he can take the pig by the tail and swing it. Toto agrees, calling the bear "old monster," and leads him back to the cottage, shouting "Granny, Granny!" The eggs are for a party that night, to be used in a custard, with Mr. Baldhead, Jim Crow, and Ger-Falcon attending. Toto also notes Bruin has no tail and shares memories of building a snow fort with him.

The narrator invented frog-dumplings in soup as a surprise for Toto and Madam, but Toto choked and Madam became ill at the thought, though neither ate it; <DW53>, Cracker, and the narrator enjoyed the soup alone. The bear prepares and serves the soup, watches the patient with satisfaction, and is described as pleasant when standing with a clean cloth over his arm, head on one side, and face beaming with pride. The raccoon and Toto prepare the table with a clean cloth, cups, plates, and bowls. A large quantity of high-quality honey is stored in pots and laid in a tree’s crotch; bees attack both the raccoon and Bruin, the latter having a bee fly into his eye, causing him to let go of the raccoon’s feet, leading to the raccoon’s fall through the hollow tree, which he describes as a falling star. The raccoon is protected by fur and covers his nose with mullein-leaves tied with grass. The narrator finds a pungent paper package containing ginger, which causes a burning sensation in mouth, nose, throat, and stomach, prompting the narrator to seek and drink water from a tin basin. The bear and <DW53> attempt to reach a honey hive in a tree by having <DW53> stand on the bear’s head, with the bear holding his feet. The bear later plays games with Toto and <DW53>, and invites them to supper, during which he eats three watermelons. The raccoon expresses a saving disposition and notes bees add a pungent flavor to honey.

Chop-Chin, identified as Nai-Ping, the second priest of the Saki-Pan, delivers the Celestial Footstool to the royal palace at ten o'clock at night, having been sent by the Chief Cabinet-maker to prevent profane eyes from seeing it. The Footstool, which the cabinet-maker had repaired all day and broke during a previous incident when Celestial Majesty struck a Putter-on-of-Slippers, is protected from profane gaze and changes color if touched. The sentinel, stationed outside the palace, opens the bronze gates after being told by Chop-Chin that the bundle is the Celestial Footstool, despite warnings that touching it results in four hundred lashes. The sentinel, though alarmed, allows the boy to pass, saying "Pass on, in the name of the Dragon." As Chop-Chin approaches, one of the four sleeping guards stirs, sees the boy’s white robe, and demands, "Who goes there?" The boy then hurries away into the darkness.

A boy with a snow-white tunic and an unbraided pig-tail walks along a well-paved street toward the Great Temple of the Golden Dragon, carrying a bronze bowl on a sacred mission. His face and figure are described as of singular beauty, and he stops at the temple's great bronze gate. A bear is confused about the boy's pig-tail, questioning how a pig's tail can be worn on the head, and contrasts it with a pig in a sty. The grandmother explains that a Chinaman wears a pig-tail, a cultural practice. Meanwhile, a pig is described as singular and has never left its sty, only going into the yard by the cow-shed; Toto confirms this and notes the pig does not care to go out often. Toto then follows a raccoon and exits the yard, walking, running, leaping, and scrambling toward the forest.

Miss Mary recounted an adventure involving a raccoon, a parrot, and <DW53>, who confirmed the raccoon was gone after a pleasant ride and showed him the way, bidding him goodbye without a promise to return. Miss Mary thanked <DW53> for saving her, Madam, and Cracker’s lives, noting they had not been good friends recently but hoped their relationship would improve. Mr. Ger-Falcon, introduced by Bruin as a friend, arrived in a hostile manner but is now trusted. Toto, a boy, revealed that Mr. Ger-Falcon is actually Mr. Chicken Hawkon, who attempted to carry off Toto’s Black Spanish chickens the previous morning due to being starving. Mr. Chicken Hawkon saw the chickens as food, agreeing with Toto that chickens are eaten when they grow up. The boy breathed relief upon hearing the story, praised <DW53> and Miss Mary, and would give Miss Mary a golden nose-ring if she had a nose.

Toto, a loyal and joyful companion, stays with the narrator and grandmother, settling in a cottage where he performs daily chores and shares peaceful forest outings with them. The bear, Bruin, is a friend who initially resists the idea of shaving but eventually joins in laughter after Toto’s loud, joyful outburst, ending with a shared "caw" from a distant crow. In a separate setting, Chop-Chin, a twelve-year-old boy, is too young to work as a sweeper, as the law requires at least fourteen years of age; he visits the imperial court-yard where sweepers are excitedly discussing a fatal accident. The bear and raccoon recall a famous autumn honey-hunt that was disrupted by an accident, which provided their winter’s supply of honey. Toto inquires about scrubbing-shoes, which are described as shoes with stiff bristles used by sweepers to scrub pavements.

Snow covers the forest in thick drifts, forming strange half-human shapes and spreading smoothly like a vast counterpane, with tall trees draped in white feathery masses that fall on Toto and his companion as they push aside branches and brambles. The snow is soft, powdery, and delightful, and the air is fresh, crisp, and mild, indicating a shift in weather. The hermit observes that snow is melting, the sun shines with greater warmth, and the air is now soft, believing spring is approaching. At the cave entrance, prints of many small feet—having hopped, run, and crept from all sides of the forest—converge, having cleared brambles and creeping vines. A man claims cows are ignorant of such matters, recounts swinging on a cow’s tail, and was kicked off without words, calling it “kicked, Toto! I give you my word for it. Kicked me!” A squirrel says it would have done the same in the cow’s place.

The Golden Dragon disappears, causing the priests to experience intense terror, fall flat on their faces, and chant "We slept!" believing it left because they were asleep. They express desolation, awaiting death, and later sing of its return, praising it for bringing glory, beneficence, and peace. A loud metallic clang and knocking at the Temple door alert the priests, who open the door to find black guards peeping through, reporting the Dragon sitting on its hind-legs and knocking. The priests rush to open the bronze gates and bring the Dragon back. Eileen follows Granny’s path, moving quietly toward the door with a soft, snoring voice. The old woman had numerous old household items, including a cow, kitchen, pantry, and pots. The guards prostrate themselves before the Dragon, and Chop-Chin feels cold, golden floor beneath him. The door is shut by attendants after them.

A young cow is deeply saddened when her calf is taken away, roaring all day and mowing to express her grief. She asks the Oldest Ox about a moon-calf, which he says lives in the moon and is still a calf regardless of its origin. The Ox claims people frequently take calves to the moon and states that if a creature is called a calf, it is a calf, even if it is unusual. He avoids answering further questions to prevent brain fatigue and pretends to sleep. The young cow, thinking intensely, stumbles against the door and wall before walking into Old Brindle's stall, where she is prodded by horns. The farmer's boy believes the cow is sick and plans to give her a warm mash and cut an inch or two off her tail. The moon shines brightly, turning the world silver, with icicles glittering like crystal spears and snow sparkling like diamond-dust.

The master, a central figure, plays a lively air on the fiddle, directing the group’s movements and praising the bear’s performance during forward and back steps. He instructs the bear to stand straighter, the raccoon to point his toe, and the <DW53> to hold his head up and not look at his tail. The fellow, described as having a hooked nose, straggling red beard, and little green eyes twinkling with an evil light, eats hastily in the cozy kitchen without using knife or fork, unseen by the bright eyes of the parrot and raccoon. The raccoon believes no one of his size will attend the waltz and will partner with Toto, while Bruin feels it is a misfortune to be large, though Pigeon Pretty and the grandmother value his strength and kindness. The grandmother, with snowy curls, a cap, kerchief, and ebony stick, is admired by Toto. The crow addresses Lady Parrot (Miss Mary) as a distinguished person, noting the chill evening, and declares the day the least happy of their lives. The group dances a quadrille to Toto’s fiddle, and the evening ends with all agreeing it was the merriest time, though each knows it is the last party.

The old lady, grandmother to Toto and Bruin, expresses grief over Bruin’s unexpected departure, noting that if it had been a <DW53>, she would not have been surprised, but Bruin, her faithful friend and helper, leaving seems unexpected. She prepares a basket containing nourishing food, bandages for a broken leg, and simple medicines, instructing Cracker to be in it when ready. Toto, initially concerned about Bruin alarming the poor man, proposes going together to deliver the basket, but Bruin refuses, stating Toto is not strong enough to care for a sick person and that he will go instead. Toto sees Bruin raising an axe to cut a log in the wood-shed, causing both to fall and the axe to fly to the other end. The bear broke the platter and spoiled the pie, learning that waltzing is not his forte and that a bullfrog cannot dance in a grasshopper’s nest, marking his last dancing lesson. The old lady perches a squirrel on her shoulder, goes into her room, and closes the door.

Mother Brindle is a cow who manages the herd, having lost ten calves and never showing distress over them. On the next day, when the weather is warm, the cows are driven to the pasture, where they enjoy honey-clover seasoned with buttercups and dandelions, stand in a cool stream under willows, and lie in the shade of an oak-tree, except for the young red cow. The young red cow believes her calf, Bossy, was taken to the moon and becomes a moon-calf, calling out to the full moon and hearing a distant "There," then runs to Mother Brindle, who rebukes her for being excited and risking milk production that would harm the herd. Mother Brindle, upon realizing milking-time, greets the neighbor. She later runs home and eats warm mash before others, becoming ill. The little maid and the princess both pass through moss and meadow, with the maid reaching a dark forest and knowing she is saved. A raccoon notes that Chucky’s aunt lives near an oak-stump with moss, where her burrow is located.

Chop-Chin, a boy, seeks entry to the Temple of the Holy Dragon on behalf of Tong-Ki-Tcheng, a powerful prince suffering from fever in the palace. He passes through gates guarded by four steel-clad guards who ask what he seeks; each drinks from a bronze bowl and promises prayers for Tong-Ki-Tcheng’s recovery and for Chop-Chin’s safe passage. After crossing a court paved with ivory and silver, Chop-Chin reaches the third gate made of whitest ivory, which leads to the Temple—the House of Gold—where the Holy Dragon, the most sacred idol in China, dwells. The gate is forbidden to profane hands; only by speaking does it open. Chop-Chin raises the bronze bowl and recites the incantation "Ka Ho Yai! Yai Nong Ti! Tong-Ki-Tcheng Lo Hum Ki Ni!" The gates open to reveal four priests in cloth-of-gold robes with golden censers. The chief priest rebukes Chop-Chin for his unauthorized presence, but he kneels and offers the bowl. The priests are later found asleep, and the chief priest, by right of Tong-Ki-Tcheng’s illness, authorizes a prayer for recovery.

Poor Chucky slept through winter and succumbed to sleep for months; the bear and raccoon played ball with him until the ball fell into a soup-kettle with hot water, causing Chucky to make a miserable squeak, after which the grandmother forbade the game, knit a red-worsted cover for him, and placed him in a cupboard by the fireplace, wishing him pleasant dreams. The bear finds reading books senseless, believing eyes can be used for other purposes, and suggests the hermit try passing winter differently, which he considers best when alone. The hermit plays back-gammon with himself using his right hand against his left, and once taught the crow, but the crow could not lift the dice-box and only threw dice by running into it, upsetting the pieces and abandoning the game due to lack of trust. The bear claims sucking one's paw is the best way to sleep and has missed it sadly this winter. Cracker enjoyed winter festivities, moving between groups, greeting friends, and sharing stories about a wonderful life with Bruin and <DW53>. The hawk is not gone; it has been asked by the master to stay for the winter and is bound by Bruin to keep the peace, so it will not hurt the crow.

The princess, described as wise, graceful, and gentle with black hair like a raven's wing and eyes like stars in clear water, can make only three remarks: "What is the price of butter?", "Has your grandmother sold her mangle yet?", and "With all my heart!" She cannot participate in court sports or dances and responds to all marriage offers—including emperors, kings, and princes—with the latter question, fixing her deep radiant eyes on the suitor. When encountered by robbers, she replies with "Has your grandmother sold her mangle yet?", causing them to gasp "It is true!" and fall into supplication. The robber chief, upon hearing her reply, turns pale, stumbles, and offers ten thousand sapphires (each as large as a pullet's egg), promising to become her slave if she accompanies him. The robbers, recognizing her, lower their weapons and lead her to their chief, a giant with a full armory, who also responds to her remark with awe. The princess, though silent in the presence of the king, ultimately says "With all my heart!" to a gallant knight, indicating a rare moment of personal connection.

The red cow, known as Bossy, is called by a distant voice and runs toward the moon, leaping over haystacks, trees, and clouds, eventually overshooting it and landing on the other side, where she is never seen again. She believes James promised her warm mash, which she thinks will be the best thing for her, and this belief motivates her journey. She claims her calf, also named Bossy, has been taken to the moon and is now a moon-calf, and she begs Mother Brindle to help retrieve him. The black cow disputes this, stating that no calves exist in the moon and that the red cow’s wits are in the moon. The sky is described as ablaze with stars, sparkling with winter radiance seen only in cold weather. Toto and his companions walk homeward in high spirits, noting the stars and crisp air, while the squirrel and raccoon look upward at the sky, with Cracker pointing to a comet. The red cow becomes a moon-cow and disappears from sight.

Toto asserts that cows do not roar but only low, citing the poem "The lowing herd winds slowly o'er the lea" and explaining that "moo" is a low sound, not low in volume. The squirrel disputes this, claiming he does not see lowness and believes there is nothing to see, and was startled by a cow's roar, falling off her horn into the hay. Madam intervenes to clarify the matter, smoothing the ruffled fur and calming the group. Bruin believes it is impossible for a man of his build to jump and change feet and tells Toto not to do it. Toto demonstrates the jump and change feet manoeuvre, showing Bruin how to perform it correctly, and notes that <DW53> has already mastered it. <DW53> observes Bruin’s mistake and begins to practice the move with ease. The squirrel jumps to the clock, sits on it, and inspects his black feet, declaring they are fine and will work well.

The speaker expresses uncertainty about their friendship with <DW53> but remains magnanimous, shaking paws and welcoming him, who insists on leaving past matters behind and seeks to be introduced to the bride. The speaker notes the kettle was helpful but criticizes creatures with no self-respect for lying still without attempting to rise, stating they would not assist such beings. The bear is described as large, shaggy, and initially savage, having frightened the hermit by stealing his honey; he now claims to have intended to enter a cave gently, using one paw and then his nose, and wonders if there’s a way to be less frightful. The bear observes that humans and Madam have no hair on their faces, except a little on the top of their heads, which gives them a gentle expression. The raccoon describes the kettle as sly and secretive, pretending to be dead to be carried and cared for.

The retired butterman, who had saved money from his trade and planned to open a public house, claimed the throne as a king during a time when rulers were sought. Though no one suspected him of being an impostor, the princess recognized a familiar question and felt uneasy, causing him to become nervous and shake. He descended from his throne, invited her to a side chamber, and begged her not to reveal his secret. He offered her a bag of rubies, stating it contained six thousand rubies, each as large as a pigeon's egg, as a token of esteem. The princess accepted the rubies graciously, concluding a butterman could make as good a king as any. In another scene, a golden altar studded with rubies, sapphires, and emeralds displayed a fifteen-foot-tall idol made of pure gold, with diamond-tipped scales, two rubies in its eye-sockets, and a crown of emeralds. The ground near a fire was soft and warm, and a tall black mass unlike grass or trees stood before a fireplace. A hawk claims it cannot dig with its short beak, while a bear questions its ability, leading to a discussion about digging.

Hundreds or thousands of tiny creatures, including woodmice (old and young, big and little, with family members like cousins, uncles, aunts, and grandmothers), field-mice resembling well-to-do farmers, kangaroo-mice leaping on long hind-legs and admired by those with short legs, moles (some with plain black velvet, others with rose-stars at the end of their noses, the latter being very aristocratic and honored by woodmice), and squirrels (Grays, Reds, and Chipmunks) in full force, were seen together at an event. The woodmice, squirrels, and others including Mr. and Mrs. Titmouse, old Mrs. Shrew and her daughters, attended. Toto suggested wearing scrubbing-shoes with four brushes attached to the grandmother’s feet, a proposal accepted by the raccoon, who winked at Toto. The old man’s son’s father would wear out no more scrubbing-shoes. His Celestial Majesty desired to taste the morning air. Bruin awoke from a sound sleep due to lively fleas, then yawned, felt sleepy, noted it was not morning, and took another nap. Eily could not get her nap due to staying and keeping others talking until the doctor returned, and had extremely bad aches. Toto changed from a jig to a waltz and danced with <DW53> to the admiration of all.

The blind grandmother, confined to her little cottage, reflects on her companions—the friends who have comforted her and pine for their free wildwood life. She fondly recalls <DW53>'s mischievous but trustworthy paw, Cracker's merry chatter, and expresses affection for Mary and Pigeon Pretty, asking to stroke their feathers. She trusts Woodchuck enjoyed his visit and deeply values Bruin, calling him "dear, my good, faithful, true-hearted Bruin," though Bruin is absent when asked for a farewell. The friends, including the squirrel, raccoon, and bear, exchange half-merry, half-sad farewells around the cottage, with the squirrel noting it is not truly good-by, as they will return. The bear, busy splitting wood, says he would have said good-by if he meant to, but cannot leave the boy or grandmother. Meanwhile, a princess arrives at the palace gate, dusty and burdened, seen by the young king, who is amazed and offers help. The new king, who arrived the day before and claimed to rule, is crowned after the old king left no heir; the people welcome the princess and insist on leading her before him. The hawk contrasts the boy’s eating of tame, confiding creatures with its own snatching from strangers out of hunger.

The bear, working with never-tiring energy and good-will, washed, cooked, churned milk, and scrubbed the room. The stew was made from bread, milk, honey, baked apples, and included onions. Toto knocked on the grandmother’s room, called out, and announced supper was ready; the blind grandmother emerged with a squirrel, greeted everyone, and felt refreshed after a nap. She appeared ten years younger than the previous year and had not enjoyed such a pleasant life in many years. The raccoon worked hard, swept, dusted, tasted food to check flavor, caught rats, teased the cow, pulled the parrot’s tail, and tried to make things pleasant. The maid recognized a moon-calf and boxed a young man who was talking to her, after which he left in a huff; the cow heard this and wondered what moon-calves were and whether they were like her calf. The cow offered her bells to Cracker, but they were too big; Cracker joked about jumping over her back and balancing on her horns, asking why she doesn’t live in the house. Toto stated a cow cannot live in the house because she is too big, Granny would not like it, and cows are entirely different from wood-creatures.
